introduction-bridging-the-sql-and-nosql-.core: NewSQL rebuilds the database from scratch (consensus replication, distributed transactions, careful timekeeping) so you no longer have to choose between ACID SQL on one box and scalable but eventually consistent NoSQL.

first_principles.problem: For years the choice was binary. SQL gives transactions and joins but can't spread writes across servers. NoSQL spreads writes but gives up transactions and often consistency. Domains like payments and inventory need both correctness and scale.
truths: Read replicas don't scale writes, because every write still hits one primary.
Correctness-critical domains can't accept eventual consistency.
Consensus algorithms let a group of machines agree safely.
derivation: Split data into ranges and spread them across nodes, which **scales writes**.
Replicate each range with **consensus** (Paxos/Raft), which keeps it **correct and available** through failures.
Coordinate multi-range changes with **distributed transactions**, which keeps **ACID**.
Keep a **SQL interface** so applications don't have to change how they think.

analogy.title: Many filing cabinets that act as one
analogy.story: A classic database is one perfectly organised cabinet. NoSQL is many cabinets that don't always agree. NewSQL is many cabinets with a strict protocol: every drawer is mirrored in three cabinets that vote on each change, and a coordinator makes multi-drawer changes happen all at once.
analogy.breaks: Voting cabinets in one room agree instantly. Across regions every vote is a long network round trip, so NewSQL writes are slower than a single box.

example.title: "Why not Postgres with replicas?"
example.scenario: A payments company's write volume exceeds the largest Postgres primary.

steps.label: Replicas
steps.detail: They add read capacity only, and every payment write still goes to one primary.

steps.label: NewSQL
steps.detail: Payment rows live in many ranges on many nodes, each with its own Raft leader, so writes scale out.

steps.label: Correctness
steps.detail: Transfers touching two ranges stay atomic via distributed commit.

example.outcome: write capacity grows with the cluster without giving up transactions.

points: Replicas scale reads, NewSQL scales writes.

check.q: What does NewSQL scale that read replicas can't?
check.a: Writes. They're distributed across many nodes via sharded ranges and consensus instead of one primary.

the-google-spanner-revolution.core: Spanner shards data into key-range tablets, replicates each with Paxos across zones, lets you pin data to regions, and orders transactions globally with TrueTime.

first_principles.problem: Google needed one database across hundreds of data centres, holding petabytes, serving millions of requests per second, and with a strict guarantee: if transaction A commits before B starts, everyone in the world sees A before B. No existing system offered all of that.
truths: Data must be split to scale, and splits must move as data grows.
Any replica may fail, so a majority must agree on writes.
Laws and latency both care where data physically lives.
derivation: Split tables into **tablets by key range**, auto-split and rebalanced, with no manual resharding.
Replicate each tablet with **Paxos**: a write commits when a majority accepts it.
**Geo-partition**: pin rows to regions for GDPR and low latency.
Solve global ordering with **TrueTime** (next lesson).

analogy.title: An international library network
analogy.story: Books are grouped by shelf ranges (tablets), and each range is held by three branches in different cities that vote on every change (Paxos). European readers' books stay in European branches (geo-partitioning). New shelves are split off automatically as a range grows.
analogy.breaks: Libraries can tolerate a branch being a day behind. Spanner can't, because every committed write must be visible in the correct order everywhere.

example.title: EU users' data stays in the EU
example.scenario: A global app must keep EU citizens' rows in EU data centres.
flow: EU ranges placed in EU zones

steps.label: Placement
steps.detail: Rows for EU users are partitioned and their replicas are placed only in EU regions.

steps.label: Replication
steps.detail: Each EU tablet has replicas in several EU zones voting via Paxos.

steps.label: Benefit
steps.detail: Compliance plus low-latency reads for EU users.

example.outcome: one logical database that respects data residency and survives zone failures.

check.q: Why does Spanner need a majority, not all replicas, to commit?
check.a: So the system keeps working when a minority of replicas is down or slow, while still guaranteeing any two majorities overlap.

truetime-spanners-secret-weapon.core: TrueTime admits clocks are uncertain and bounds the error (ε, a few ms) with GPS and atomic clocks. Spanner then waits out ε before acknowledging a commit, so timestamp order equals real-time order.

first_principles.problem: Server clocks drift. If T1 commits on server A at 10:00:00.100 and T2 on server B at 10:00:00.050, you can't tell which really happened first. Without trustworthy time, you can't order transactions globally.
truths: No clock is exact, but its error can be bounded.
Better hardware (GPS, atomic clocks) means a smaller bound.
If you wait longer than the error bound, the ordering is no longer ambiguous.
derivation: Return time as an **interval** `[earliest, latest]` that's guaranteed to contain true time.
Keep ε tiny (< 7 ms) with **GPS and atomic clocks** in every data centre.
On commit, take a timestamp and **wait until `TT.after(ts)` is true** (commit wait).
Now any transaction that starts later gets a larger timestamp: **external consistency**.
Pay about ε of extra latency on every write.

analogy.title: Waiting out a stopwatch's error
analogy.story: A race official's stopwatch is accurate to ±5 ms. To be certain runner A finished before runner B started, the official waits 5 ms after A's finish before signalling B's start. Then no measurement error can make the order look reversed.
analogy.breaks: An official can use one stopwatch. Spanner has thousands of servers, which is why it needs synchronised GPS/atomic hardware everywhere to keep ε small.

example.title: A commit with ε = 4 ms

steps.label: Wait
steps.detail: Block until every server's `earliest` is past 108, which takes roughly 2ε.

steps.label: Ack
steps.detail: Now report success. Any transaction that starts afterwards must get a timestamp > 108.

example.outcome: global real-time ordering, at the cost of a few milliseconds per write.

points: TrueTime = time as a bounded interval.

check.q: Why does Spanner's commit latency depend on clock quality?
check.a: Commit wait lasts about the uncertainty ε, so a less accurate clock means a longer wait on every write.

cockroachdb-spanner-for-everyone-else.core: CockroachDB brings Spanner's design to commodity hardware: ranges replicated with Raft, hybrid logical clocks instead of atomic clocks, Postgres wire compatibility, and serializable isolation by default.

first_principles.problem: Spanner needs Google's GPS and atomic-clock infrastructure and runs only on Google Cloud. Most teams want the same guarantees on their own servers or any cloud, without special hardware.
truths: Ordinary servers only have NTP-synced clocks.
Consensus algorithms can run on any hardware.
Causality (A caused B) can be tracked in software.
derivation: Shard data into **ranges**, each replicated by **Raft** (elected leader, replicated log, automatic re-election).
Replace TrueTime with **hybrid logical clocks**: (physical time, logical counter), advanced on every message.
Handle the remaining clock uncertainty by **restarting** transactions when needed.
Offer **serializable** isolation by default and a **survivability** model: RF=3 survives 1 failure, RF=5 survives 2.
Speak the **Postgres wire protocol** for easy adoption.

analogy.title: A club without a master clock
analogy.story: Every member writes their own time on each note, and whenever they receive a note stamped later than their own watch, they move their watch forward to match. Causes are always stamped before their effects, even though nobody has a perfect clock.
analogy.breaks: Club members can just ask when unsure. CockroachDB restarts the transaction when a value falls inside the clock-uncertainty window, which adds latency.

example.title: Pinning a table to the US
example.scenario: Compliance requires US customer data to stay on US nodes, across 3 US zones.

steps.label: Constrain
steps.detail: Configure the table's zone to `+region=us-east` with 3 replicas.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Raft replicas sit in 3 US zones, so losing one zone keeps the range available.

code.text:
ALTER TABLE customers CONFIGURE ZONE USING
  num_replicas = 3, constraints = '[+region=us-east]';

example.outcome: Spanner-style resilience and placement on ordinary infrastructure.

points: Raft instead of Paxos: same goal, easier to reason about.
HLC instead of TrueTime: causal order, occasional restarts.
Serializable by default, Spanner is externally consistent.

check.q: Serializable vs external consistency, what's the difference?
check.a: Serializable means transactions appear in *some* serial order. External consistency additionally requires that order to match real-time order.

tidb-separation-of-powers.core: TiDB splits the database into independently scalable layers: stateless SQL servers, a Raft-replicated key-value store (TiKV), and a placement brain (PD), plus TiFlash columnar replicas for analytics.

first_principles.problem: In a monolithic database, compute and storage scale together: you can't add query-processing power without adding storage, or the reverse. Many MySQL shops also want to scale out without rewriting their apps.
truths: Query load and data size grow at different rates.
Stateless services are trivial to scale horizontally.
Analytical scans want columnar storage, while transactions want row storage.
derivation: Make SQL parsing, planning and execution a **stateless layer** (TiDB servers) behind a load balancer.
Store data in **TiKV**: regions replicated by Raft, with transactions via Percolator-style two-phase commit.
Centralise metadata and scheduling in the **Placement Driver** (PD, backed by etcd).
Add **TiFlash** columnar replicas kept in sync via Raft for **HTAP**.
Speak the **MySQL protocol** to minimise migration effort.

analogy.title: A restaurant with separate front of house, kitchen and manager
analogy.story: Waiters (TiDB servers) take orders and can be added on busy nights without touching the kitchen. The kitchen stations (TiKV) hold and prepare the food, each mirrored for safety. The manager (PD) decides which station handles what. A separate prep line (TiFlash) prepares big catering orders without slowing the kitchen.
analogy.breaks: Waiters and kitchen are in one building. TiDB layers talk over the network, so each query pays extra hops compared with a single-node MySQL.

example.title: Black Friday query spike
example.scenario: Query CPU triples for a day, while data size barely changes.

steps.label: Compute
steps.detail: Add 6 stateless TiDB servers behind the load balancer. They're ready in minutes.

steps.label: Storage
steps.detail: TiKV is untouched, so there's no rebalancing.

steps.label: Analytics
steps.detail: The sales dashboard queries TiFlash replicas, so transactional traffic isn't slowed.

code.text:
-- add a columnar replica for analytical queries
ALTER TABLE orders SET TIFLASH REPLICA 1;

example.outcome: compute scales up and down for the spike without moving data, and analytics stay off the transactional path.

points: TiKV + Raft hold the data, PD places it.
TiFlash enables HTAP, MySQL compatibility eases migration.

check.q: Why can TiDB servers be added or removed freely?
check.a: They're stateless. All data lives in TiKV, so a TiDB server holds nothing that needs moving.

choosing-between-newsql-systems.core: Pick a NewSQL system by cloud strategy, protocol and consistency needs: Spanner for managed global external consistency, CockroachDB for self-hosted Postgres-style, TiDB for MySQL migration and HTAP. Design keys to avoid hot ranges.

first_principles.problem: All three NewSQL systems promise scale with ACID, but they differ in where they run, which protocol they speak, how strong their guarantees are, and what they cost to operate. And all of them share failure modes that catch teams out.
truths: Every NewSQL write waits for a quorum, so latency is higher than single-node.
Range sharding sends sequential keys to the same range.
Self-hosting distributed databases needs real expertise.
derivation: **Spanner**: on GCP, zero-ops, strongest consistency, global users, budget available.
**CockroachDB**: self-hosted or multi-cloud, Postgres-familiar, serializable, placement control.
**TiDB**: MySQL migration, HTAP, independent compute/storage scaling.
Expect **5–50 ms** local and **50–200 ms** cross-region writes.
Avoid **hot spots**: use UUIDs or hash-prefixed keys instead of auto-increment IDs.

analogy.title: Choosing a delivery company
analogy.story: All three deliver reliably. One is premium, fully managed and worldwide (Spanner). One you can run with your own vans anywhere (CockroachDB). One plugs into the logistics system you already have and also runs a warehouse (TiDB, MySQL + HTAP). With any of them, if every parcel is addressed to the same depot, that depot jams.
analogy.breaks: A jammed depot can hire temporary staff. A hot range is limited by its single Raft leader, and only a better key design fixes it.

example.title: A SERIAL primary key melts one node
example.scenario: An events table with `id SERIAL` on CockroachDB: one node at 100% CPU and the rest idle.

steps.label: Cause
steps.detail: Increasing IDs always land at the end of the key space, which is one range with one leader.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Use `gen_random_uuid()` (or hash-sharded indexes) so inserts scatter across ranges.

steps.label: Cost
steps.detail: Range scans by ID lose locality, so keep a separate time index if you need it.

example.outcome: write load spreads across the cluster instead of saturating one node.

points: Choose by platform, protocol and guarantees.
NewSQL writes are slower than single-node.

check.q: Why do auto-increment keys hurt range-sharded databases?
check.a: Every new key is the largest so far, so all inserts go to the same final range and its single leader becomes the bottleneck.
